content:
A tall, lumbering, hairy, barefoot creature wandering Colorado’s mountains? There had been urban legends over the ages, and from the early 1980s to 1989, stories had been quietly proliferating in the Green Mountain Falls area and Ute Pass about something a little bit strange. Sometimes it was covered in long black hair, other rare times it was gray or blond.

Then, in 1988-’89, Dan Masias and his son made national news when they reported spotting two creatures in the woods outside their cabin on Hondo Avenue in Green Mountain Falls. The first sighting, they said, was huge footprints right outside. Later that night they investigated and said there were two hairy, look-like simians, leaving through the woods in the dark.

As their alerts spread, other area neighbors went public for the first time about growling sounds, something knocking on doors and strange noises close by. In one case, there was a cabin break-in with long arm hairs caught in the screens. Later testing by a laboratory concluded the hair could be from a primate.

Schoolchildren in Green Mountain Falls admitted that they avoided walking near the “Sasquatch House” and the Hondo Avenue address during that time. Featured online are the childhood memories of R J Gurley, who grew up nearby.

There was fun to be had with all the now-named bigfoot activities. A Bigfoot sighting meter sat outside in the area and a “Bigfoot Crossing” sign had a spot on Pikes Peak Highway. For some years tourists were greeted by a Sasquatch tourist novelty shop in Manitou Springs.

The “sightings” stories even drew a television “Unsolved Mysteries” visit here and an episode with no official conclusions or film. Over the decades, curious visitors have continued to arrive and investigate who’s on that mountain or not. Through it all there has never been a humanoid body or authentic photograph found, no Bigfoot, no Sasquatch, no Yeti.

Besides the “Unsolved Mysteries” filming, possibly the most famous visitor to the Hondo Avenue cabin was paranormal investigator Jon-Erik Beckjord, whose Crypto-Zoology Museum of strange things was in Malibu, Calif.

According to his extensive Wikipedia, he had attended two years at the Air Force Academy and graduated in sociology from Tulane University. He had been a city planner before tiring of that work and focused on chasing the paranormal. He opened his first California museum in 1989, but it burned down, including his “creatures of fact or fancy.” For a time he had a Bigfoot, UFO and Loch Ness Monster Museum in San Francisco that closed.

Cynics and investigators had for years ridiculed him. Following a gathering of believers, one curious man was invited by Beckjord for a five-day tracking trip. The man reported they had seen nothing, absolutely nothing but trees and leaves and shadows before he left. When Beckjord returned, he reported that indeed the day he was alone he had seen a Bigfoot crossing the road.

There was laughter about Beckjord’s visit to Scotland to see the Loch Ness Monster. He sought fame through television and radio guest appearances as the paranormal expert.

Before his death in 2008, Beckjord repaired electrical appliances as Captain Neon and had a third collection of oddities in North Beach, Calif., that was dubbed the city’s “strangest museum.”

Well-documented beliefs in a creature in mountainous areas and the wilderness go far back to early times, even to pioneers and gold prospectors who had scary tales of “wild men” or “mountain devils.” Native Americans had reported seeing hairy humanoids. Indigenous British Columbia tribes had been frightened by Sasq’ets, later called Sasquatch. There had been story lore elsewhere about The Abominable Snowman or Yeti in the Himalayas and Asia as well.

Bigfoot/Sasquatch legends seemed to have restarted in the 1950s at a logging site in Bluff Creek, Calif., when a bulldozer operator saw 16- to 18-inch footprints with a 5-foot stride. It was reported in what was purported to be a letter from an unnamed reader and the area newspaper, the Humboldt Times, said the footprints belonged to what they appropriately named Bigfoot. The bulldozer fellow had made plaster footprint casts, according to the Humboldt County Historical Society.

Immediate worldwide interest in the story erupted and the newspaper writers followed it with more of their creative Sunday morning feature stories. Only later it was revealed that a road contractor had carved big wooden feet for the tracks to prank folks.

In 1967, Bluff Creek struck again, with a blurry photo of a huge, hairy, upright-walking female that found its way onto YouTube. And Humboldt County gained bigfoot murals, competitions and a 20-foot-tall wood creation at a building containing Bigfoot collections.

Years later a photographer named Bob, or maybe his family, reportedly confessed he had worn a gorilla suit for the photo.

Reports of possible sightings of the legendary creature, usually only footprints, continue even today through a website, The Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization (bfro.net), which has tallied more than 130 in Colorado, but no authentic photos. Quirky tourist attractions include one in Bailey outside Denver, The Sasquatch Outpost, with one of the big, hairy creations standing right outside. And in Colorado Springs there’s a Sasquatch cookie company. Add to that movies and books and tall tales.

Top Colorado county saw-ones have come from Park County, Teller County, Lake County (a knock on the front door in the woods), and seven from El Paso County, too. In the 2000s was a report from people near the route of the Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad.

The state with the most reported sightings has always been the heavily wooded, lightly populated Washington, followed far behind by California, Oregon, Michigan and Florida.
